strategy_name: ADX/DMI trend-strength directional gate
mechanism: when ADX>25 the market trends in the DMI-dominant direction and only that direction should be traded; below 25 the market is range-bound
setup_summary: Trade long only when +DMI > -DMI and ADX > 25; short only when -DMI > +DMI and ADX > 25. ADX rising through ~15-23 flags a trend developing; ADX falling from ~32 toward 25 flags a trend ending. ADX below 25 = range-bound, no directional edge.
trigger_invalidation: Directional thesis invalid when ADX drops back below 25 (trend weakening/ending — not necessarily reversing) or when the DMI pair flips.
risk_geometry: Regime gate, not an entry; no stops/targets specified; pairs with any entry system; usable as higher-timeframe bias.
quote: the ADX line suggests that the market is trending in the direction of the greater DMI line if it is above 25. If it is below 25, it suggests that the trend is weak or range bound.

strategy_name: Relative-strength rotation across a universe (RRG)
mechanism: cross-sectional relative strength and its momentum rotate clockwise around a benchmark; long the strong-and-strengthening, short/avoid the weak-and-weakening
setup_summary: For each element in a universe compute RS ratio vs benchmark (JdK RS-Ratio) and RS momentum (JdK RS-Momentum). Long/overweight elements crossing into the top-right quadrant (ratio>100, momentum>100); short/underweight elements crossing into the bottom-left quadrant (ratio<100, momentum<0). Ignore elements circling near the benchmark (100,100) — those are not where the moves are. Rotation trails confirm direction and pace.
trigger_invalidation: Rotation thesis invalid if momentum crosses back through 100 without the ratio following (rotation within a quadrant, RS>100 or <100 stays); exit when the element rotates into the opposite quadrant.
risk_geometry: Weekly/monthly hold for institutions or intraday (RRG works on any timeframe); trails of 3-17 weeks confirm rotation; book gives no stops/targets; the long top-right / short bottom-left pair is cited as the 'least risk' variant because both RS states are confirmed.
quote: the average excess return of the underperform recommendations was significantly higher than the excess return of the outperform recommendations.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 2, 'The JdK RS-Ratio and JdK RS-Momentum' and 'Relative Rotation Graphs' (pp. 65-82)

strategy_name: Higher-timeframe trend permission filter (bias before trigger)
mechanism: lower-timeframe entries are gated by a higher-timeframe trend state; short-bar moves that contradict the larger timeframe are mostly noise and should not be acted on
setup_summary: Choose a bias interval larger than the trigger interval: e.g., monthly/weekly DMA channel (6-period high/low averages displaced 4 bars) as bias for daily DMA triggers; weekly ENS/EROC as bias for daily signals; Kase Permission Stochastic builds synthetic bars (e.g., 5 daily bars rolled into one synthetic weekly) so permission is granted ~2 bars earlier than waiting for the natural higher-timeframe close. Take only long triggers when bias is long, only short triggers when bias is short; when the filter grants opposite permission, require stronger bar-pattern confirmation before entry.
trigger_invalidation: A bias flip reverses the permissioned side and warrants reevaluation of open positions; Kase's trend-direction principle: each smaller cycle is a test of the next larger cycle.
risk_geometry: No entry/stop/target of its own — it gates which signals are admissible. Kase prefers the filter at ~3x the traded bar length (synthetic). Dow 30 study: adding monthly-DMA bias to daily DMA triggers raised W/L from 0.59 to 7.0 and return per trade from 0.29% to 7.40%; GE study: moving-with-bias 168.88% vs ignoring-bias -66.42%.
quote: Bias indicators are primarily set to intervals larger than those used to trigger in and out of trades.

strategy_name: Squeeze-play: extreme sentiment as setup, price as trigger
mechanism: extreme bullish/bearish positioning (options ratios, short interest) creates reversal fuel that only fires when price confirms; an overcommitted crowd leaves no one left to continue the trend
setup_summary: Setup: excessive bearish options betting (high put/call median) or excessive bullish (high call/put median); high short interest in an uptrend (short-squeeze fuel) or depressed short interest in a downtrend (long-squeeze fuel). Trigger: price closes through the daily DMA channel in the setup's direction. Both sentiment and price must agree; a sentiment setup is never traded without a price trigger.
trigger_invalidation: Setup invalid if sentiment is not extreme or if price fails to trigger; position exits on the reverse DMA-channel cross. 'We always use a price study to activate the sentiment setup.'
risk_geometry: Entry/exit on DMA-channel cross. Worked examples: BBY long triggered on close above DMA after mid-March put/call extreme; DIA short triggered on drop below DMA in early May after April call/put extreme. No ATR stop given.

strategy_name: Intraday value-line and opening-range bias
mechanism: prior-session value levels (pivot/support/resistance) and the opening range define the day's bias; price breaking them reveals who is in control and the day's momentum
setup_summary: At session start, set resistance/pivot/support value lines from prior-day structure plus the first-hour (or first 5-min) opening-range high/low. Price above the resistance line => long-only bias; below the support line => short-only bias; between them => neutral. Break of the opening-range high => positive near-term bias; break of the opening-range low => negative. Clusters of value lines (e.g., prior-day last-2h high + pivot + 60-min opening low) are stronger levels. Support broken then reclaimed above the pivot = sellers failed (positive recovery); resistance taken then lost = buyers failed.
trigger_invalidation: Bias flips when price crosses the defining level; a broken level retested as the opposite side is the strong continuation pattern; levels expire at session end.
risk_geometry: Intraday, expires at session end; bias determines admissible side; value lines act as targets and pivot breaks as triggers; no ATR stop specified. Flash-crash day cited as case where a disciplined value-line approach keeps the trader on the right side.
quote: If price breaks above the first-hour high, the near-term bias turns positive. If price breaks below the first-hour low, the near-term bias turns negative.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 3, 'Erlanger Value Lines' (pp. 126-133)

strategy_name: Phase-consistent tactics: horizontal vs vertical market
mechanism: eliminate the low-probability side first: in an uptrend the short side has near-zero probability of prevailing, so only long tactics are admissible; range phases require range-edge tactics
setup_summary: Classify the market as uptrending, downtrending, or sideways. Uptrend: only buy higher price pivot lows. Downtrend: only short lower price pivot highs. Sideways: only buy range lows / short range highs, or stand aside. If no admissible entry appears, do not trade — standing aside is often the best choice. Most losses come from being on the wrong side of the phase or using the wrong tactic for the phase.
trigger_invalidation: The tactic table is re-evaluated when the phase changes; a phase change requires reclassification before any new entry.
risk_geometry: Entry at pivot lows/highs or range edges on the allowed side; framework-level tactic table (Table 5.1), no explicit stops/targets.
quote: The highest possible high-probability trade starts with the mind-set and very basic rules of: In an uptrend, don't be short; in a downtrend, don't be long.

strategy_name: Probe and Pullback (breakout-retest from balance)
mechanism: a probe beyond a balance extreme exhausts resting orders; a pullback that holds the balance extreme/HVA then reasserts in the probe direction
setup_summary: After a defined horizontal balance (>=2 relatively equal pivot highs and lows), price probes beyond one extreme, then retraces back to or into the balance area. Entry in the probe direction on a stall in the retest zone, i.e. between the broken balance extreme and the HVA boundary; expectation is that the retest of the balance extreme or HVA leads to reassertion in the probe direction and a directional move.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: retest of the broken balance extreme or HVA after a probe, with a stall signal (smaller-degree balance/support indication) in the zone. Invalidation: retracement through the entire HVA of the balance area - 'a retrace through the entire HVA of the balance area invalidates the setup'; a full retrace converts the trade to the Reversal-and-Retest premise.
risk_geometry: Entry on bar close anywhere between the retested balance extreme and the HVA limit (long: extreme-to-HVA lower limit; short: extreme-to-HVA upper limit); stop beyond the opposite extreme of the HVA; first target the probe extreme, then far side of the next low-volume hole / beyond the balance area on phase transition.
quote: The retest of the balance area after the 'probe' outside of balance should not retrace any further than the HVA of that balance area.

strategy_name: Reversal and Retest (failed probe -> reversal on retest)
mechanism: when a probe fails and price pierces the HVA of the balance area aggressively, the imbalance has flipped; the reversal is confirmed by a retest of the balance range or HVA
setup_summary: When a Probe-and-Pullback fails - the pullback shows no stall and price trades through the entire HVA of the balance area in an aggressive/persistent (initiative) fashion - the setup reverses: enter on a retest of the balance range or HVA in the direction opposite the failed probe. Fading extremes of smaller-degree balances once the HVA is broken, or once the opposite balance extreme is broken, is also valid.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: initiative piercing of the HVA followed by a retest of the balance extreme/HVA. Invalidation: price reclaims the far side of the broken HVA and re-engages the original direction (no vacuum formed); per V8, still_valid = close stays on the reversal side of the frozen reference.
risk_geometry: Entry on retest after the pierce; stop beyond the opposite extreme of the HVA (often beyond the extreme of the balance reversed through for smaller structures); first target from smaller structures/balances to the left, with the best setups targeting the far side of a low-volume-at-price hole.
quote: The key to this setup is the piercing of the HVA of the balance area in an initiative way. Once broken, entries into this type of trade can be taken upon a retest of the range or of the HVA.

strategy_name: Fast-Trigger momentum turn with time-expiry (ATM FT)
mechanism: a fast momentum oscillator turning up from oversold / down from overbought biases price in the turn direction for ~7.58 bars (empirically 66.32% of closes in the turn direction)
setup_summary: With a higher-timeframe trend present (TSB trend-strength line present / multi-timeframe monthly->weekly->daily alignment), buy when the fast momentum line turns up from oversold (short when it turns down from overbought). Expect price to move in the turn direction or sideways for ~7.58 bars (rounded to 8). If no favorable movement or condition change occurs within ~8 bars, exit before the price stop.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: FT turn from overbought/oversold aligned with the higher-TF trend background. Invalidation: no movement in the turn direction within ~8 bars (the new trend may not be developing); the longer-timeframe FT turning against the position adds pressure.
risk_geometry: Entry at the oscillator turn (bar close); time-stop at ~8 bars if no movement (half-cycle); initial stop outside the near-term volatility band; backtest claim: closes in the turn direction 66.32% over an average 7.583 bars (INDU, 10 years).
quote: when the ATM FT turns up or down, price will move in the direction of the turn or sideways 66.32 percent of the time for a period on average of 7.583 bars.

strategy_name: Exhaustion countertrend with condition-change confirmation
mechanism: at trend extremes, momentum exhaustion (fast and slow triggers concurrently overbought/oversold against the trend) can mark a reversal, but only if the overall market condition changes within ~8 bars; otherwise the trend resumes
setup_summary: At a mature vertical move (slowing price movement, decreased slope, overlapping retracements, divergence), look for momentum exhaustion (both fast and slow momentum lines concurrently oversold against the trend, then the fast line turns up). Enter countertrend only if the trend-condition coloring (trend bars / trend line) flips to the countertrend direction within ~8 bars, preferably before the fast line reaches the opposite extreme. If no condition change occurs within the window, the trend resumes - exit and do not add.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: exhaustion signal at an extreme (FT+ST concurrently against trend + FT turn). Confirmation: market condition change within ~8 bars. Invalidation: no condition change within ~8 bars -> trend resumes; the book explicitly warns most exhaustion signals are only a pause, and warns against reversing off a single timeframe unless price moves very fast (6-8 bars).
risk_geometry: Entry at the extreme (bar close); stop beyond the extreme/top; time-stop ~8 bars for condition change; typically used to trade around large positions (exit 20% in and out), not to reverse.
quote: If you are buying/selling exhaustion, the condition of the market must change to the direction of your position within a preset amount of time. Should no change in condition occur within that time limit, exit.

MEDIUM for perps. Distinct from the with-trend momentum-turn finding (that entry requires trend background present; this entry fades an ending trend).

strategy_name: Scale out half at profit, breakeven stop on the remainder
mechanism: Booking partial profit transfers the risk on the remaining position to zero (breakeven stop), making it structurally hard to turn a winning trade into a loser while still participating in continuation.
setup_summary: Enter with multiple contracts; when the market gives a decent profit, exit half the position; immediately move the stop to breakeven on the remainder; let the remainder ride for the continuation move. Falsifiable as a lifecycle rule: after first target, stop relocates to entry, remainder position persists.
trigger_invalidation: If the market fails after the first exit, the breakeven stop exits the remainder at zero; the trade cannot become a net loss.
risk_geometry: Entry: multiple units at one level; partial target at ~1R (decent profit); stop moved to breakeven after partial exit; remainder runs with no fixed target.
quote: Trade in multiple contracts, and get out of half of your positions when the market gives you a decent profit... If the market fails, then move your stop to breakeven so you have a chance to break even on the other half of the trade.

notes: Trade-management rule, venue-agnostic; maps to ExposureBook episode rules (partial close + stop re-peg to entry). strategy_name: Pyramiding - add to winners at fixed price increments
mechanism: In a trending move, adding units at fixed favorable increments compounds gains while using open-market profit as the risk base; early adds carry the most risk and later adds are funded by unrealized gains.
setup_summary: Take a base position near a perceived low; add one unit every fixed price increment (book: every 20 cents, equal to one margin unit) as price advances, using resting limit buy orders; trail stops up with each add based on prior support or accrued profit; exit the full book at a defined top/level. Explicitly avoid the 'reverse pyramid' of adding larger sizes at higher prices, where a small setback wipes out all profit.
trigger_invalidation: Thesis dead if the first stop is hit before any add (risk = first add); a reverse-pyramid structure is identified as ruin-prone.
risk_geometry: Entry: limit orders at fixed increments (e.g., 20c apart = one margin unit); stops trailed below prior adds; initial risk = first position's stop distance; target = analyst-defined top.
quote: You add positions every 20 cents higher... This tactic virtually trades using money made from the market rather than your own capital.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 12, 'Pyramiding' (pp.205-210)
notes: Book itself warns it is 'leveraging leverage using more leverage', exposed to margin-raise and reverse-pyramid risk. In perps, funding paid on the full growing notional and high leverage make the 'market money' framing hazardous; treat as a position-scaling variant within one exposure, gated on regime, rather than a standalone expert.

strategy_name: Pre-weekly-close trend continuation (S&P Friday 10:30 a.m. rule)
mechanism: Position-squaring and 'don't hold the bag over the weekend' behavior drives the trend formed mid-session to persist into the weekly close; margin-call and central-bank flow windows concentrate this effect.
setup_summary: US equity futures: the intraday trend formed between 10:30 a.m. and noon on Fridays becomes the trend into the Friday close; day-trade with that established trend rather than fighting it. Book shows 12 weekly closes near the daily high/low, all but two exceptions being holiday sessions. Crypto analogue would be trend persistence into the weekly candle close (Sunday 00:00 UTC) or into funding boundaries.
trigger_invalidation: Pattern broke on holiday/shortened sessions (2 of 12 examples); expects exceptions when the session structure differs.
risk_geometry: Intraday entry with the established mid-session trend; exit at close; no stated stop/target.
quote: The trend from 10:30 a.m. until 12 noon will be the trend going into the close of business on Fridays.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 12, 'Other Tactics and Techniques' (pp.212-213)
notes: The exact 10:30-noon Friday window is US-session and weekly-close specific; perps have no Friday close. A falsifiable crypto analogue (trend persistence into the Sunday 00:00 UTC weekly close, or the last hours before an 8h funding payment) could be tested, but requires defining session boundaries that V8's replay does not currently model. Gate until a time/session feature group exists.

strategy_name: Stop-reversal when the setup is too obvious (fade crowded consensus)
mechanism: When a setup is so universally recognized it 'can't fail', the information is already priced; its failure produces reversal momentum, so a reversing stop on the failed side converts the stop-loss into the entry.
setup_summary: When a signal accumulates many confirmations (book: '10 different indications') and looks unable to fail, do not enter one-sided; use a stop reversal - place a reversing stop so that if the market stops you out, you are filled in the opposite direction, letting failure momentum offset the original loss. Conceptually adjacent to the failed-breakout family (liquidity vacuum reentry): the 'everyone sees it' breakout that fails is exactly the crowded-signal case.
trigger_invalidation: Reversal thesis fails if the original side continues; risk is double-sided exposure at the reversal moment.
risk_geometry: Entry: reversing stop beyond the obvious level; risk = original stop distance; no stated target (momentum continuation).
quote: Whenever you have a signal that is so strong that you think it can't fail... then use a stop reversal... What everyone else knows isn't worth knowing sometimes.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 12, 'Other Tactics and Techniques' (p.214)
notes: Anecdotal rule of thumb; hard to feature 'crowdedness' from OHLC tape alone. Natural fit is as a refinement/variant of the existing failed_breakout family (crowded breakout -> reversal) rather than a new family. The reversing-stop mechanic also needs lifecycle work (flip direction on stop-out), which conflicts with V8's single-exposure rule; keep in backlog.

strategy_name: Buy-stop entry on channel/resistance breakout
mechanism: Price trading through a defined channel/resistance point is the market 'proving' upside; a resting buy stop converts that proof into an entry, avoiding pre-trigger commitment.
setup_summary: When price is contained in a channel/range, place a buy stop above resistance (or sell stop below support) and enter only if price trades through it; the market must prove direction by surpassing the level. This is a stop-triggered (intrabar) breakout entry rather than a bar-close entry.
trigger_invalidation: No fill unless the level is traded through; a triggered stop fills at next available price with slippage.
risk_geometry: Entry: stop order beyond the level, fill at or near stop with slippage; protective stop on the opposite side of the channel; target beyond the opposite boundary.
quote: you might place a buy stop above that area to enter a long position if the market moves that high. In other words, you are waiting until the market proves that it may go higher by surpassing a certain price or chart point.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 10, 'Stop Orders' (p.181)
notes: Relevant to V8's entry-type modeling: current experts enter NEXT_BAR_CLOSE; the stop-entry variant fills intrabar when price trades through the level (market-if-touched semantics with slippage). Perps have no gaps, so stop fills are cleaner than in futures, but fast 24/7 moves can still gap the fill. Add stop-entry fill semantics (trigger at level, fill at next price) to the canonical simulator before screening breakout families.

strategy_name: Pivot point S1/R1 reaction with candle confirmation (P3T)
mechanism: prior-period equilibrium P=(H+L+C)/3 with derived S1/S2/R1/R2 levels act as reference points where price reacts; prior support/resistance reverse roles after a breakout
setup_summary: Compute P,R1,R2,S1,S2 from the prior period HLC (daily/weekly/monthly; for 24h markets use the full-session range and combine all sessions). When price trades at or near weekly or monthly S1/R1 (strongest when weekly and monthly numbers converge), wait for a confirming reversal candle (hammer at S1, shooting star/harami/engulfing at R1), then enter next-bar-open in the reaction direction. Trade only the FIRST test of the level. Target the opposite pivot level; stop beyond the swing extreme.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: price reaches S1 or R1 within a small tolerance and a confirming candle completes. Thesis invalidation: a decisive close beyond the pivot level (level fails as reaction point); also abandon after repeated tests of the same level ('if you go to the well one too many times, the well will run dry').
risk_geometry: entry NEXT_BAR_CLOSE after reversal candle at pivot; stop = swing extreme beyond the level (below the established low / above the high, often close-only); target = opposite pivot (R1 after S1 bounce) or R2/S2; expiry = one pivot cycle (intraday for daily numbers, swing for weekly/monthly).
quote: Trading for the day will usually remain between the first support and resistance levels as these professional floor traders make their markets. As a general rule, I usually will only take a trade based off the first test of the S1 or R1 pivot number.
chapter_anchor: Ch 6, 'Finding Equilibrium' and 'P3T Signals'
notes: Book gives many worked cases (sugar monthly S1 6.09 vs low 6.11; S&P weekly S2 781.67 vs 771.30) but no statistics - practitioner heuristic. Weekly/monthly pivots are computable on 24/7 BTCUSDT with no gap distortion, and the book explicitly handles 24h markets by using the full-session range. Caveat: self-fulfilling following is a concentration risk, and high-leverage perps attract stop-hunts near round/pivot numbers. Core of the book's P3T = pivot + candle + oscillator multi-verification ('verify, verify, verify').
book: A Complete Guide to Technical Trading Tactics - How to Profit Using Pivot Points, Candlesticks & Other Indicators 2004

strategy_name: Climax volume + open-interest decline reversal (blow-off top / capitulation bottom)
mechanism: after an extended trend, an unusual volume spike with declining open interest (longs liquidating, shorts panic-covering) signals a climaxing market and a major trend reversal
setup_summary: In an established trend, price makes wider-than-normal daily swings with unusually strong volume while open interest declines. Three characteristics required for a climax top or bottom: (1) wider-than-normal range/volatility, (2) heavy volume, (3) declining open interest. Rising price + falling OI indicates short-covering rather than new longs (weakening, potential reversal). Treat as a major reversal warning and do not add to trend positions.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: volatility expansion + volume spike + OI decline over the same window at the end of a long trend. Thesis invalidation: OI resumes expansion while price continues in trend direction (new money entering = trend intact).
risk_geometry: entry after confirmation (not on the spike bar itself); stop beyond the extreme made during the climax; target = prior range/trendline; expiry = swing (days-to-weeks).
quote: if a substantial daily market price increase or decrease occurs after a long steady uptrend or downtrend and has an unusually high volume period, it is considered to be a blow-off top or bottom and can signal a market turning point or trend reversal
chapter_anchor: Ch 5, 'Volume' and 'Putting the Data Together'
notes: Refines the existing DATA_BLOCKED capitulation backlog family. Advantage over the book's futures: perp open interest is real-time (the book laments OI is published next-day), so the OI condition is directly testable; funding adds a pressure gauge the book lacks. Caveat: perp OI mixes hedgers and leveraged specs and direction is not visible in raw OI, so OI decline alone is ambiguous.
book: A Complete Guide to Technical Trading Tactics - How to Profit Using Pivot Points, Candlesticks & Other Indicators 2004

strategy_name: Inside bar / range-compression breakout
mechanism: range compression (current bar wholly inside the prior bar's range) concentrates resting orders; a breakout of the range releases them directionally with continuation
setup_summary: Current bar's high and low both within the previous bar's high-low (inside bar; close is not important). Place a buy stop above / sell stop below the inside bar's range and enter on the breakout, expecting continuation. Generalizes to triangles/pennants as continuation patterns: the time the consolidation took to form is the measuring distance, and breakouts are strongest when the pattern does NOT coil all the way to the apex.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: a bar closes whose range is fully inside the prior bar, then the next bar trades through either bound. Thesis invalidation: false breakout closing back inside the range (then treat as failed breakout); note the longer a triangle takes to form, the less power the breakout usually has.
risk_geometry: entry stop-order beyond the inside-bar extreme; stop = opposite side of the inside bar, or below the first low point forming the support line for triangles; target = measured move (formation height projected from breakout, flagpole distance); expiry = 3-5 bars intraday.
quote: The whole current range is within the previous bar's range... A breakout either way of the inside bar range gives a buy or sell signal, based on the theory that there is a continued price move in the direction of the breakout.
chapter_anchor: Ch 3, 'Bar Charts' (inside bar) and Ch 5, 'Triangle Chart Patterns' and 'Flag Formations'
notes: 1h BTCUSDT produces frequent inside bars and tight consolidations; 24/7 trading with no close-gaps makes the range bounds unambiguous. High leverage raises the cost of the false-breakout branch, so the failed-breakout exit semantics matter. This is the volatility-contraction family V8 can formalize cleanly.

strategy_name: MA crossover (golden/dead cross) and test-of-crossover as support/resistance
mechanism: short-term vs long-term moving average crosses mark trend transitions, and the crossover point itself acts as a future S/R reference because it is the price where signals were generated
setup_summary: With 3/9/18-period EMAs (or 5/10/20 weekly): golden cross (short crosses above long) = buy, dead cross = sell. Distinctive claim: markets often test the crossover point rather than the prior high/low, so a retest of a prior crossover level is a trade reference. Confluence with weekly/monthly pivots at the same price is a strong reversal setup (crude oil $31 example). Fails in ranges - the book states markets are trending only ~1/3 of the time.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: cross occurs or price returns to a prior crossover level. Thesis invalidation: whipsaw in a trading range (signals fire on every gyrating cross) - requires a trend/regime filter; exit if price crosses back.
risk_geometry: entry at cross or at retest of the crossover level; stop beyond the swing low or just past the level (silver example: buy $4.45-4.49, stop below $4.38 prior low); target = trend continuation, scale out where MAs act as support; exit discipline: at 100% of initial margin return, take half off and trail the stop on the remainder above the 3-day and 9-day MA.
quote: A lot of time you will see that a market does not rally to test the old highs but, instead, goes up to test the point of the moving average crossover.
chapter_anchor: Ch 8, 'Moving Averages'
notes: Directly relevant to V8's existing trend_pullback family (already consumes ema_fast/ema_slow). The distinct refinement is the 'test-of-crossover as S/R' behavior and the pivot/MA confluence gate. Standalone cross trading on 1h BTCUSDT would whipsaw in ranges; use as a trend filter / existing-family variant rather than a new active expert.

strategy_name: Oscillator divergence (MACD / stochastic) - false-extreme reversal
mechanism: price makes a new extreme while the momentum oscillator makes a weaker extreme - the move lacks participation and is a false/fragile extreme prone to reversal
setup_summary: Bullish divergence: price makes a lower low vs a prior low while stochastics/MACD makes a higher low (false bottom). Bearish divergence: price makes a higher high while the oscillator makes a lower high (weak top). Stochastic rules: %K crossing below %D above 70 with both pointing down = hook sell; %K crossing above %D below 30 with both pointing up = buy. Works in volatile/choppy conditions; oscillators give false signals in steady trends. Confirm with pivot target or candle pattern before acting.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: divergence forms at a pivot S/R or after an extended trend. Thesis invalidation: in strong trends oscillators stay overbought/oversold and keep generating false signals (book: during a whole downtrend stochastics kept printing buy signals; only the >75% cross was the classic sell).
risk_geometry: entry after price confirmation (%K/%D cross or confirming candle); stop beyond the extreme of the divergent bar; target = prior extreme or pivot; expiry = 1-2 days for swing use.
quote: This is a condition where the market price makes a low that is lower than a previous low but the underlying MACD pattern makes a higher low. This divergence indicates that the low is weak or a false bottom... and signals a potential price reversal.
chapter_anchor: Ch 8, 'Stochastics' and 'Moving Average Convergence/Divergence'
notes: Computable on 1h BTCUSDT but premature in strong perp trends; fits the existing V8 vocabulary as a response feature (oscillator response to price). Backlog candidate whose edge must be tested against trend-following baselines before formalization.
book: A Complete Guide to Technical Trading Tactics - How to Profit Using Pivot Points, Candlesticks & Other Indicators 2004

strategy_name: 8-to-10 new records exhaustion (consecutive new-high/new-low streak + reversal candle)
mechanism: after 8-10 consecutive new highs or new lows the trend has run its course; a reversal candle appearing within 1-2 bars of the 8th-10th record confirms exhaustion
setup_summary: Count consecutive sessions (bars) that print a new high (uptrend) or new low (downtrend). When the count reaches the 8-10 band and a reversal candle (hammer, doji, shooting star) appears within one or two bars, fade the trend: after the 8th-9th new low, buy with a close-only stop below the lowest low; after the 8th-9th new high, sell with a close-only stop above the highest high. The stop is close-only because 'if the market truly is ready to turn around, it should not close below the established low.'
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: streak count in the 8-10 band AND reversal candle within 1-2 bars. Thesis invalidation: bar closes beyond the extreme (close-only stop); streak extends past ~10 records; also the inverse pattern can recur (book shows the 8-10 setup repeating on the dollar index downtrend).
risk_geometry: entry NEXT_BAR after confirmation candle; stop = close-only below the lowest low / above the highest high; target = prior consolidation or trendline; expiry = swing; 'the longer the time period, the longer the trade signal may work' (weekly charts give longer trades than daily).
quote: when the market price either advances or declines by making eight to ten new highs or lows, it can signal that the advance or decline should subside... put a stop close-only order below the lowest low
chapter_anchor: Ch 4, 'Reading Candle Charts' (8 to 10 new records)
notes: Novel, fully quantifiable (streak counter is deterministic) and frequent on 1h BTCUSDT. The close-only stop maps exactly to V8's bar-close semantics. Falsifiable: measure whether streaks in the 8-10 band with a reversal candle precede reversals more often than baseline. Candidate for screening as a counter-trend family with tight heat cap.
book: A Complete Guide to Technical Trading Tactics - How to Profit Using Pivot Points, Candlesticks & Other Indicators 2004

strategy_name: 1-2-3 W-bottom / M-top swing breakout (confirmed by close through the reaction extreme)
mechanism: a failed retest of a prior extreme (higher low on retest) followed by a close through the reaction high confirms accumulation and triggers a reversal breakout; measured objectives come from the head-and-shoulders neckline projection
setup_summary: W bottom (1-2-3): after a downtrend, price makes a low (1), rallies to a reaction high (2), retests the low WITHOUT undercutting it (3 = higher low), then closes above the reaction high (2) -> buy signal. Inverse M top: price makes a high (1), falls to an interim low (2), rallies below the prior high (3 = lower high), then closes below the interim low (2) -> sell. Head-and-shoulders variant: entry on neckline break; measured objective = distance from shoulder highs (or head) to the neckline projected from the neckline.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: close through the point-2 reaction extreme (not an intraday spike). Thesis invalidation: retest undercuts the prior low (higher-low premise broken, becomes continuation); close back through the breakout level.
risk_geometry: entry NEXT_BAR after the confirming close; stop below point-1 low (or point-3 low) / above point-1 high; target = measured objective (leg distance, or H&S neckline projection); expiry = swing.
quote: the price falls back again to retest the low but does not go as low as the previous low (point 3), followed by another price rally that goes beyond the first reactionary high, generating a buy signal
chapter_anchor: Ch 5, 'M Tops, W Bottoms, or 1-2-3 Patterns' and 'Head-and-Shoulders Tops or Bottoms'
notes: Structurally matches the existing DATA_BLOCKED breakout_retest backlog family. Close-based confirmation suits V8's bar-close model and avoids intraday fake breaks. The H&S measured-move is a secondary pattern (more subjective; lower priority).
book: A Complete Guide to Technical Trading Tactics - How to Profit Using Pivot Points, Candlesticks & Other Indicators 2004

strategy_name: No Cost-Basis Anchoring (the stock does not give a damn)
mechanism: the market outcome is independent of the price you paid, who recommended it, or your entry reference; anchoring hold/exit decisions to cost basis or P&L produces irrational continuation of losing exposures
setup_summary: Exit and hold decisions must be functions of the thesis and the market, never of entry price or unrealized P&L: 'a stock does not know you own it, the price you paid, who recommended it, the prices someone else paid... the stock does not give a damn.' 'You do not have to make it back the way you lost it' - do not extend a losing exposure to claw back a loss (the USAir preferred write-down).
trigger_invalidation: The rule itself is the guardrail: a position whose thesis is dead must exit regardless of whether P&L is negative or positive, and a position whose thesis is alive must be held regardless of how good the entry looks now.
risk_geometry: Stop and target are derived from structure and thesis, not from entry price; dead-thesis (still_valid) exit is computed independently of unrealized P&L.
quote: A stock does not know you own it, the price you paid, who recommended it, the prices someone else paid . . . the stock does not give a damn.
chapter_anchor: 1995 'Stocks' (USAir write-down: 'you do not have to make it back the way you lost it')
notes: Directly supports V8's separation of the stop exit from the dead-thesis (still_valid) exit and mandates that lifecycle exit conditions never reference entry price or P&L.
book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

strategy_name: Line of least resistance regime gating
mechanism: trade only in the direction of the dominant market trend; stand aside in cash when the market is consolidating sideways
setup_summary: First classify the market regime from price structure on a multi-bar/swing horizon: uptrend, downtrend, or sideways consolidation. Take longs only when the line of least resistance is up, shorts only when it is down; when the market is sideways, hold cash and wait for a clear direction to establish. Entry comes only after the trend is visible in price action, never in anticipation.
trigger_invalidation: No trade is taken while the market is sideways and undecided; a position's thesis dies if the regime classification flips against it (trend breaks).
risk_geometry: No explicit stop/target stated for this rule; risk is controlled by refusing to trade against the regime plus the separate 10% per-position loss cap.
quote: Always evaluate and appraise general conditions first, and determine the line of least resistance. Is it an upward-trending market or a downward-trending market? Or is it consolidating—moving sideways, trying to make up its mind?
chapter_anchor: Ch. 3 'The San Francisco Earthquake Rumbles in New York' (pp. 53-54); codified as rule 1 in Ch. 4 'The Crash of 1907' (p. 66)
notes: Maps to V8's absent-by-default regime filter: it enters only through a registry experiment beating the simpler baseline on frozen OOS, never as a permanent gate. For BTCUSDT 1h the up/down/sideways classification is directly computable from OHLC structure with no lookahead.
book: Jesse Livermore - World's Greatest Stock Trader 2001

strategy_name: Ride the big swing; sell the loser, keep the winner
mechanism: expected value concentrates in long-trend continuation; banking small profits early and funding losers by cutting winners destroys the edge
setup_summary: Once a position is established with the line of least resistance and confirmed, hold it through normal corrections; exit only when the basic trend visibly changes, not to bank small gains ('you can't go broke taking a profit' is explicitly rejected as a losing philosophy). When margin forces a reduction, close the losing position first and keep the winning one. Big money comes from the big swings; small point-clipping only served to build the original stake.
trigger_invalidation: Exit signal is a change in the line of least resistance / basic trend reversal, not an adverse wiggle and not a profit target; the thesis must visibly break.
risk_geometry: Entry: as the probe/pyramid method; stop: 10% cap; target: open-ended ride of the swing (no fixed R-multiple); expiry: none - position ends on trend change.
quote: The big money was in the big swings, in waiting for the basic trend to play out and riding the stock for as long as possible... Always sell the loser, keep the winner; he knew the rule, but he did not act on it.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 4 'The Crash of 1907' (p. 66); Ch. 5 'The Cotton King' (p. 93)
notes: Directly relevant to V8's trend_pullback family: target_r 1.0 + expiry 8 bars may be too small to capture 'the big swing'; suggests thesis-based (still_valid) exits over fixed small R-targets, and a lifecycle rule that winners are never cut to fund losers. Any change must challenge the frozen OOS baseline first (registry discipline).
book: Jesse Livermore - World's Greatest Stock Trader 2001

strategy_name: News-reaction asymmetry (bad news discounts slowly in a bull regime)
mechanism: identical news moves price differently by regime; in an uptrend negative news is initially absorbed and prices rebound, so the tradable turn appears only when price action confirms the regime change, not on the news itself
setup_summary: After a major negative exogenous event (e.g., the 1906 San Francisco earthquake) during an established uptrend, expect the initial shock to be absorbed and prices to rebound to former levels (Livermore went flat, made nothing on the initial move). The short thesis becomes actionable only when the market thereafter fails to advance - rallies falter and stocks slide back from old highs - then short/add into the failing rally. Trade the price reaction to the event, never the event itself.
trigger_invalidation: If after the event price keeps making new highs and holds, the reaction thesis is invalidated; a violent one-day shock drop alone is not the signal (Livermore was 'flat on the trade' after the initial shock move).
risk_geometry: Entry: short on failed rally / break of the prior low after the event (bar-close basis); stop: 10% cap; target: ride the new downtrend; no fixed expiry.
quote: Livermore knew that bad news in a bull market climate takes a lot longer to sink in with the public than bad news in a bear market, when the climate is already negative.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 3 'The San Francisco Earthquake Rumbles in New York' (pp. 59-60); the confirmation principle it implements is 'To anticipate the market is to gamble; to be patient and react only when the market gives the signal is to speculate' (p. 54)
notes: Single anecdote, so NARRATIVE evidence, not a candidate for an active expert. In 24/7 perp crypto with high leverage and near-instant information flow, news is discounted faster, weakening the 'slow sink-in' asymmetry; still, regime-dependent reaction to exogenous events is a testable feature input for the response feature group (e.g., post-shock rally-failure detection as a location/response feature).
book: Jesse Livermore - World's Greatest Stock Trader 2001

strategy_name: Leverage-forced-selling cascade and stress correlation collapse
mechanism: Leverage converts a loss into forced selling; when many leveraged players hold nominally diversified positions, the common forced-sell channel makes every asset/spread fall together, so diversification is illusory in stress ('You don't sell what you should. You sell what you can.').
setup_summary: Standing risk rule: cap aggregate exposure whose exit requires buying/selling into a stressed market, because in a forced-sell regime every leg unwinds simultaneously - LTCM was 'buying the stuff that everyone wanted to sell' in every market, so its assets 'would be susceptible to falling in unison if a time came when literally everyone wanted to sell.' A per-instrument/direction exposure cap is insufficient; assumed correlation across strategies/venues must spike toward 1 under funding spikes or liquidation cascades.
trigger_invalidation: n/a - this is a standing cap. The correct reaction to a stress signal (funding spike, liquidation volume, spread blow-out) is to reduce, not to add.
risk_geometry: Heat cap / correlated exposure cap; any liquidity-provision-style trade must carry an explicit exit plan because liquidity 'is a straw man' - there is no liquidity for the community as a whole, and if you are not in debt you cannot be made to sell.
quote: You don't sell what you should. You sell what you can.
chapter_anchor: Ch.3 'On the Run', pp.41-43; Rosenfeld liquidity-provision admission pp.44-45
notes: The 1994 rout (Steinhardt losing $800M in four days, Soros $650M in two) and LTCM's 1998 collapse are the book's core evidence that spread trades that are 'balanced enough to be safe' all break together when the same leveraged owners are forced to sell - direct support for V8's correlated exposure cap and for treating diversification claims with suspicion.

strategy_name: Beauty-contest pricing of non-producing assets
setup_summary: Structural framing: BTC produces nothing, so its price is set by the Keynesian beauty contest - what matters is what others believe others believe ('rising prices create their own excitement... the neighbor gets rich'). Consequence for BTCUSDT 1h: herding/trend persistence is a first-order dynamic that can run far beyond any 'fair' value, and fundamental-value anchors are unavailable; both momentum persistence and crowd-following risk are amplified.
trigger_invalidation: Standing framing; implies trend/momentum families should expect long persistence tails, and 'value'-anchored mean-reversion should not assume a fair-value magnet.
risk_geometry: None stated.
quote: you are betting not on whom you believe to be the prettiest contestant, but who others will believe is beautiful
chapter_anchor: 2012 annual meeting, 'The Three Categories of Investment' (Keynes, General Theory ch. 12)
notes: Supports the expectation that herding persistence dominates BTCUSDT and cautions the capitulation backlog against any intrinsic-value anchoring.

strategy_name: Counter-trend pullback against a 50-day MA trend (with trend-side hedge)
mechanism: Trends lumber in fits and spurts while counter-trends are swift, brief retracements that lose momentum and revert to the trend
setup_summary: Define trend by the 50-day moving average (close below 50MA = bearish, above = bullish). In an established trend, trade counter-trend pullbacks actively with liberal stops, while a trend-side position (book: an option) accumulates value along the trend; exit the counter-trend leg the moment its momentum fades.
